One-Off 1971 Plymouth Road Runner RTS Pops Up for Sale After 7 Years
19 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
When it comes to classic Mopars, collectors usually hunt the Hemi-powered cars . These cars are rare regardless of the nameplate and model year. However, some Mopars don't need Hemi powerplants to be ultra-rare. The Rapid Transit System cars, for instance, are one-off creations.
What's a Rapid Transit System vehicle, you ask? Well, back in 1970, Plymouth put together a traveling promotional road-show that was supposed to market its muscle cars to young buyers across the US. It was called the Rapid Transit System (RTS) Caravan and visited auto shows, dealerships, and race tracks through 1970 and 1971.
The cars were based on Plymouth's existing models, but they were heavily modified, especially in terms of body work. The concept vehicles, which were true one-of-ones, were customized by various designers.
The 1970 lineup included a Road Runner, a Duster 340, and a six-barrel Cuda . For 1971, Plymouth repainted the Duster and the Cuda while introducing a 1971 version of the Road Runner. When the RTS program ended after the 1971 auto show season, some cars found their way into private hands, while others disappeared.
Three of the four vehicles were eventually tracked down and purchased by renowned collector Steven Juliano. One by one, he acquired the two Road Runners and the 1970 Duster. The fourth car, the 1970 Cuda, remained hidden in a garage for nearly 50 years. It resurfaced in 2023 and sold for a whopping $2.2 million.
As for the Juliano-owned RTS cars, they were auctioned off in 2019, when his entire estate was sold following his passing. The 1970 Road Runner sold for $341,000, while the 1970 Duster changed hands for $264,000. The 1971 Road Runner went under the hammer for $236,000. It's been seven years since then, and the latter is up for sale again.
The one-off 1971 Road Runner was recently included among the lots that will cross the block at Mecum's Kissimmee 2027 auction in January. The car is still unrestored and in pristine condition, just like it was when it left Juliano's estate.
Built by Chuck Miller of Styline Custom for Chrysler Corporation in 1970, the Road Runner RTS sports an extended front end that's six inches longer than the standard Road Runner. It also has a hand-formed steel mesh grille, flanked by dual horizontal lenses concealing a quad headlamp layout.
The Mopar was also fitted with Ram Air induction scoops, clear taillight lenses, and a recessed deck lid. Miller deleted the steel bumpers and fitted custom black wheels. The Orange Candy paint is complemented by custom pearl white stripes running the entire length of the body. The 3D Road Runner heads on all four fenders serve as side market lights.
The interior remained unchanged, while the drivetrain is a very basic 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8 mated with a three-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission. This powerplant came standard on the Road Runner in 1971.
How did this car soldier on in such fabulous condition without a restoration? Well, unlike the other RTS cars, this one remained with its builder for decades. Chuck Miller kept the Road Runner until the early 1990s, likely pampering it and keeping it safe from the elements. He then sold the car directly to Steven Juliano.
How much will it fetch? Mecum doesn't provide an estimate as of this writing, but it's safe to say that it will get a lot of attention at Kissimmee 2027. It should sell for a higher sum than it did back in 2019, and I have a feeling that the final bid could exceed $400,000.
